title: The Journey of a Plastic Bottle
summary: How a plastic bottle is made from oil, where it goes after use, why plastic lasts so long, and how reducing, reusing, and recycling help.
poll: Recycling is the best way to solve the problem of plastic waste.

versions.title: Where Do Bottles Go?
versions.text:
Look at this bottle. It is made of plastic. It holds cold water. But where does it come from? Where does it go?

Most plastic comes from oil and gas. They are deep in the ground. A big factory turns the oil to small beads. Then the beads melt. A machine blows air in. Pop! Now it is a bottle.

You drink the water. Then you toss the bottle. Where does it go? It may go to a plant. There it is made new. It may go in a big pit in the ground. Or it may be litter. Wind and rain can take it to the sea.

Plastic lasts a long time. Tiny things in the soil eat old food. They do not eat plastic. The sun breaks it up. But the bits stay. A bottle can last for hundreds of years. Birds and fish may eat the bits. That can hurt them.

We can recycle bottles. A truck picks them up. They get cleaned and cut up. Then they melt. They are made into new things. One is a shirt.

You can help. Use less plastic. Reuse a bottle. Fill it each day. Put old bottles in the recycle bin.

versions.title: A Bottle's Trip
versions.text:
Look at a plastic bottle. It holds cold water on a hot day. But where does it come from? And where does it go?

Most plastic is made from oil and gas. They come from deep in the ground. In a big factory, the oil is made into small beads. The beads melt. Then a machine blows them into the shape of a bottle.

You drink the water. Then you toss the bottle. Now what? It may go in a bin to be made into something new. It may be dumped in a big hole in the ground. Or it may end up as litter on a beach or in the sea.

Plastic lasts a long, long time. Tiny living things in the soil cannot eat it. The sun breaks it into bits, but the bits stay. A bottle may last for hundreds of years. Sea birds and fish can eat the bits by mistake.

We can recycle a bottle. Trucks take it to a plant. There, it is cleaned and cut up. The bits melt and are made into new things, like a shirt or a new bottle.

You can help. Use less plastic. Reuse a bottle you can fill. Put old bottles in the recycle bin.

versions.title: A Bottle's Long Trip
versions.text:
Look at the plastic bottle in your hand. It keeps your water cool on a hot day. But where did it come from? And where will it go next?

Most plastic is made from oil and natural gas. They are found deep under the ground. In a factory, the oil is turned into tiny beads. Later, the beads are melted. A machine blows air into the soft plastic. It takes the shape of a bottle.

After you drink the water, you throw the bottle away. Then what? It might go to a place where it can be made into something new. It might be buried in a big hole called a landfill. Or it might become litter on a beach, in a river, or in the sea.

Plastic lasts a very long time. Tiny living things in the soil break down food and leaves. But they cannot break down plastic. Sunlight cracks it into small bits. But the bits do not go away. A bottle may last for hundreds of years. Sea turtles and birds may eat the bits by mistake.

The good news is that we can recycle bottles. Trucks carry them to a plant. Workers and machines sort them. The bottles are washed and cut into flakes. The flakes melt. They become new things, like shirts, carpets, or new bottles.

You can help. Use less plastic. Reuse a bottle that you can fill again. And always put empty bottles in the recycling bin.

versions.title: The Journey of a Plastic Bottle
versions.text:
On a hot day, a cold bottle of water feels wonderful. But have you ever thought about where that plastic bottle came from? Or where it will go when you are done with it? Its journey is longer than you might think.

Most plastic is made from oil and natural gas, which are found deep underground. In a factory, chemicals from the oil are joined together and formed into tiny beads. Later, these beads are melted and pressed into a small tube. The tube is heated, and air is blown inside it. The soft plastic stretches to fill a mold, and it becomes a bottle.

After you drink the water, the bottle starts a new journey. It might go to a recycling center. It might be buried in a landfill, a huge pit where trash is dumped. Or it might become litter. Wind and rain can carry litter into rivers, and rivers carry it to the sea.

Plastic is strong, and it lasts a very long time. Tiny living things in the soil can break down food scraps and leaves, but they cannot easily break down plastic. Sunlight cracks it into smaller and smaller pieces, but the pieces do not disappear. A bottle may last for hundreds of years. Sea turtles, birds, and fish sometimes eat these pieces by mistake.

Luckily, plastic bottles can be recycled. First, they are collected. Next, they are sorted and washed. Then they are chopped into flakes. Finally, the flakes are melted and turned into new things, such as clothes, carpets, and new bottles.

Everyone can help. Use less plastic. Reuse a bottle you can fill again. Recycle the bottles you do use.

versions.title: The Journey of a Plastic Bottle
versions.text:
On a hot afternoon, a cold bottle of water can feel wonderful. But have you ever wondered where that plastic bottle came from? Where will it end up when you are finished with it? Its journey is much longer than most people imagine.

Most plastic is made from oil and natural gas. These are pumped from deep underground. In a factory, chemicals from the oil are linked together into long chains and formed into tiny beads called pellets. Later, the pellets are melted and shaped into a small tube. The tube is heated until it is soft, and air is blown inside it. The plastic stretches to fill a mold. In seconds it becomes a bottle.

Once the bottle is empty, it begins a new journey. It might travel to a recycling center. It might be buried in a landfill, a huge pit where trash is dumped and covered with soil. Or it might become litter. Wind and rain can carry litter into rivers, and rivers carry it all the way to the sea.

Plastic is strong and light, and it lasts a very long time. Tiny living things in the soil decompose food scraps and fallen leaves. But they cannot easily break down plastic. Sunlight slowly cracks plastic into smaller and smaller pieces. The tiniest pieces are called microplastics. They never truly disappear. A bottle may last for hundreds of years. Sea turtles, birds, and fish sometimes swallow these pieces by mistake.

Luckily, plastic bottles can be recycled. First, trucks collect them. Next, workers and machines sort them and wash them. Then the bottles are chopped into small flakes. Finally, the flakes are melted and turned into new products, such as clothing, carpets, and even new bottles.

Everyone can help protect the planet by following three words: reduce, reuse, and recycle. Reduce the plastic you use, because a bottle that is never made never becomes waste. Reuse a bottle that you can fill again and again. And when you do use a plastic bottle, put it in the recycling bin.

versions.title: From Oil to Ocean: A Bottle's Journey
versions.text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, few things feel better than a cold bottle of water. Yet most people never stop to think about where that plastic bottle came from or where it will go once it is empty. The answer is a journey that can last far longer than a human lifetime.

The story begins deep underground. Most plastic is made from oil and natural gas, which are known as fossil fuels. At a factory, chemicals taken from these fuels are linked together into long chains. The new material is formed into tiny pellets that look like grains of rice. At a bottle plant, the pellets are melted and shaped into small tubes. Each tube is then heated and placed inside a mold, and air is blown into it. The soft plastic stretches to fill the mold and becomes a bottle.

After a few minutes of use, the empty bottle faces several possible futures. It may be collected and sent to a recycling center. It may be buried in a landfill, where trash is piled up and covered with soil. Or it may become litter. Wind and rainwater can wash litter into rivers, which carry it to the sea.

Plastic is useful because it is strong and light, but that same strength causes a problem. Tiny living things such as bacteria decompose food scraps and leaves, but they cannot easily break down plastic. Sunlight and waves only crack it into smaller pieces. The smallest of these pieces are called microplastics. Scientists believe a bottle may last for hundreds of years. Sea turtles, seabirds, and fish sometimes eat plastic by mistake.

Recycling gives bottles a second life. Bottles are collected, sorted by type, and washed. They are then shredded into flakes, which are melted and made into new products such as clothing, carpets, and new bottles.

The best plan follows three words: reduce, reuse, and recycle. Reduce the plastic you use, reuse a refillable bottle, and recycle the plastic you cannot avoid.

versions.text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, few things feel more refreshing than a cold bottle of water. Yet most people never pause to consider where that plastic bottle originated or where it will travel once it is empty. The answer is a remarkable journey that can last far longer than a human lifetime.

The story begins deep underground. Most plastic is manufactured from oil and natural gas, which are known as fossil fuels. At a chemical plant, substances extracted from these fuels are linked together into extremely long chains called polymers. Water bottles are usually made from a polymer known as PET, which is formed into tiny pellets that resemble grains of rice. At a bottle factory, the pellets are melted and shaped into small tubes. Each tube is then reheated and placed inside a mold, where a powerful blast of air inflates it. The softened plastic stretches to fill the mold and becomes a finished bottle within seconds.

After only a few minutes of use, the empty bottle faces several possible futures. It may be collected and transported to a recycling center. It may be buried in a landfill, where garbage is piled up and covered with layers of soil. Alternatively, it may become litter. Wind and rainwater can wash litter into rivers, which eventually deliver it to the sea.

Plastic is valuable because it is strong, lightweight, and waterproof, but that same durability creates a serious problem. Microscopic organisms such as bacteria decompose food scraps and fallen leaves, but they cannot easily break down plastic. Sunlight and waves merely degrade it into smaller fragments, and the tiniest of these fragments are called microplastics. Scientists estimate that a single bottle may persist for hundreds of years. Sea turtles, seabirds, and fish sometimes swallow plastic, mistaking it for food, which can injure or even kill them.

Recycling provides bottles with a second life. Bottles are collected, sorted by type, and washed to remove labels and dirt. They are then shredded into flakes, which are melted and manufactured into new products such as clothing fibers, carpets, and new bottles. However, researchers estimate that only a small portion of all the plastic ever produced has been recycled.

The most effective strategy follows three words: reduce, reuse, and recycle. Reduce the amount of plastic you use, reuse a refillable bottle, and recycle the plastic you cannot avoid. Reducing comes first, because a bottle that is never manufactured never becomes waste. A single refillable bottle can replace hundreds of disposable ones.

versions.title: The Long Life of a Plastic Bottle
versions.text:
On a scorching summer afternoon, few things feel more refreshing than a chilled bottle of water. Yet most people rarely consider where that plastic container originated or what becomes of it once it is empty, even though the answer involves an industrial and environmental journey that can continue for centuries.

The story begins deep underground, because most plastic is manufactured from petroleum and natural gas, the fossil fuels that also power many cars and power stations. At a chemical plant, small molecules extracted from these fuels are bonded together into extremely long chains called polymers. Water bottles are usually made from a polymer known as PET, which is formed into tiny pellets resembling grains of rice. At a bottle factory, the pellets are melted and molded into small tubes, and each tube is later reheated, placed inside a mold, and inflated with a powerful blast of air until it stretches into a finished bottle.

Once the bottle is empty, its future depends largely on human choices. It may be collected and transported to a recycling facility, or it may be buried in a landfill, where garbage is compacted beneath layers of soil. Alternatively, it may become litter, and wind and rainwater can carry discarded plastic into rivers that eventually deliver it to the ocean.

Plastic is valuable precisely because it is strong, lightweight, and waterproof, but this durability creates a serious environmental problem. Bacteria and other microorganisms readily decompose food scraps and fallen leaves, yet they cannot easily digest the long polymer chains in plastic. Instead, sunlight and waves gradually degrade a bottle into progressively smaller fragments, and the tiniest of these are called microplastics. Scientists estimate that a single bottle may persist for hundreds of years, and marine animals such as sea turtles and seabirds sometimes swallow plastic after mistaking it for food.

Recycling can give bottles a second life. Collected bottles are sorted by type, washed to remove labels and dirt, and shredded into flakes, which are melted and manufactured into products such as clothing fibers, carpets, and new bottles.

Nevertheless, researchers estimate that only a small portion of all the plastic ever produced has been recycled. For that reason, environmental experts emphasize the familiar order: reduce first, then reuse, and recycle what remains. A refillable bottle can replace hundreds of disposable ones.

LOW.modelAnswer: My family can reuse a refillable water bottle instead of buying new plastic ones. MID.modelAnswer: Plastic bottles can be a problem for the environment for a couple of important reasons. One detail is that plastic does not easily decompose the way food scraps do, so a bottle thrown away in a landfill can stay there for hundreds of years without breaking down completely. Another detail is that sunlight and waves only crack plastic into tiny pieces called microplastics, which animals like sea turtles and fish can accidentally eat. Even though bottles start as small plastic pellets at a factory, once they become trash they create a problem that lasts far longer than most people realize, which is why it helps so much to reduce how many bottles we use.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say that recycling is enough to solve the plastic bottle problem. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I disagree that recycling alone is enough to solve the plastic bottle problem, because the evidence shows plastic causes damage even before and after it reaches a recycling center. Plastic bottles are made from petroleum, a fossil fuel formed into a long-chain polymer that is intentionally durable and strong, which is exactly why it does not easily degrade once it becomes trash; a single bottle may persist for hundreds of years, slowly breaking into harmful microplastics rather than disappearing. In addition, many bottles never reach a recycling center at all, instead becoming litter that washes into rivers and oceans, so recycling programs cannot address plastic that was never collected in the first place. Because durability makes plastic both useful and dangerous, I believe reducing and reusing bottles matters just as much as recycling them.
